entities.summary:
The Allied invasion of Italy, also known as Operation Avalanche, was a pivotal event in World War II that took place on September 17, 1943, in the Salerno region of Italy. This invasion was the first major Allied campaign on the Italian mainland, marking a significant turning point in the war.

The invasion was led by American, British, and Canadian forces, who landed on the beaches of Salerno and advanced inland towards the city of Naples. The campaign was marked by intense fighting, with the Allies facing stiff resistance from German and Italian forces. Despite these challenges, the Allies eventually secured the city of Naples and pushed the Germans back towards the north.

The Allied invasion of Italy had far-reaching consequences, leading to the eventual liberation of Italy from German occupation and paving the way for the Allied invasion of Southern France. The campaign also marked a significant shift in the balance of power in Europe, as the Allies gained a foothold on the continent and began to push the Germans back.

The invasion of Italy remains one of the most significant events of World War II, with its legacy still felt today in the region. As General Mark Clark, the commander of the Allied forces, once said, "The capture of Naples was a major turning point in the war in Italy," and it marked the beginning of the end of the German occupation of the country.
